newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan rebels poised to capture capital.
newsitem.headline: Afghan rebels poised to capture capital.

text.p: Afghanistan's rebel Taleban Islamic militia appeared poised to capture Kabul on Friday as defenders loyal to President Burhanuddin Rabbani were reported pulling out of the besieged capital.

Taleban sources in neighbouring Pakistan said the militia had seized the main government airbase at Bagram, 50 km (30 miles) north of Kabul after taking parts of the capital, including its disused Khwaja Rawash airport.
There was no immediate independent confirmation of these reports, but witnesses in Kabul said government forces appeared to be abandoning the capital they had vowed to fight to their death to defend.
The Taleban sources said the militia had also taken Kabul's Soviet-built Microrayon housing complex in the east and the diplomatic Wazir Akbar Khan district in central Kabul.

The sources, quoted by the Pakistan-based Afghan Islamic Press (AIP), said troops loyal to President Rabbani were fleeing northwards, but his militia forces were resisting Taleban fighters near the presidential palace in central Kabul.
There was no immediate independent confirmation of the report, which also said the Taleban had taken Kohe Asmai hill, known as Television Hill, in the middle of Kabul.

While the airport in Kabul was made unusable by factional fighting, the Soviet-built Bagram, shared by jet fighters and civilian airliners, was the only base left giving the government an air link with the outside world.
On Thursday night much of the city resembled a ghost town with streets virtually deserted except for small groups of government soldiers trudging through the streets.

There were only sporadic exchanges of machine-gun and small arms fire heard from the edges of the city. The security ministry building had been abandoned and at least six tanks and several trucks full of troops had been seen leaving the city.
Some civilians had fled the city on the road north earlier in the day in dozens of trucks and buses, but with a curfew in force most Kabul citizens stayed in their homes.
In the Wasir Akbar Khan diplomatic quarter, small groups of residents came onto the streets to burn posters of President Rabbani and his military chief Ahmad Shah Masood.
There was no information about the whereabouts of Rabbani, Prime Minister Gulbuddin Hekmatyar and military commander Ahmad Shah Masood.

The Taleban, which emerged from obscurity two years ago and now controls most of Afghanistan, seeks to oust Rabbani and impose a strict Islamic order. Its leader Mullah Mohammad Omar said recently it had no ethnic or regional prejudices and only wanted to enforce Islamic sharia (law).

Earlier on Thursday, the official government spokesman, Amrullah, told reporters it would fight to the death to defend the capital. "We are establishing defences in every street of Kabul," he said as the two sides fought in the outskirts.
Amrullah accused Pakistan of sending military technicians to help the Taleban and said other countries, which he refused to name, were also aiding the rebels.

Pakistan denied the accusations. "We have had and will continue to observe total neutrality while we must maintain a close watch on the events as they develop," a Pakistan Foreign Ministry spokesman said in Islamabad.
An official of the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), Jan-Luc Paladini, said there had been hundreds of dead and wounded on both sides in the past two days.
The ICRC on Thursday stopped all flights from Bagram to the Pakistani city of Peshawar after evacuating 50 people, including 16 ICRC delegates, leaving only staff needed for emergencies.
"The ICRC is staying in Kabul. We are not leaving," he said.
